question.text: What does managing risk mean for a driver?

answer.text: Managing risk means driving aware, predictable, smooth and skilled, and building safe habits on purpose until they become your normal style.

teaching.text: Managing risk means aware, predictable, smooth and skilled driving with habits built on purpose. Remember: aware, predictable, smooth, skilled.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Managing risk means driving aware, predictable, smooth and skilled, and building safe habits on purpose until they become your normal style.

question.text: What are the common factors in fatal crashes?

answer.text: The common factors in fatal crashes are speed, impairment, distraction, unbelted occupants and inexperience.

teaching.text: Speed, impairment, distraction, unbelted occupants and inexperience are the common fatal crash factors. Remember: speed, impairment, distraction, belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The common factors in fatal crashes are speed, impairment, distraction, unbelted occupants and inexperience.

question.text: Which age group faces vehicle crashes among its leading causes of death?

answer.text: In Washington, vehicle crashes are among the leading causes of death for people aged sixteen to twenty-five, a group more prone to fatal and serious injury crashes.

teaching.text: Crashes are among the leading causes of death for people aged sixteen to twenty-five. Remember: young drivers face highest risk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In Washington, vehicle crashes are among the leading causes of death for people aged sixteen to twenty-five, a group more prone to fatal and serious injury crashes.

question.text: What is risk awareness?

answer.text: Risk awareness is the ability to spot present and possible hazards, including other road users, weather and distractions, so you can change what you do before a crash.

teaching.text: Risk awareness means spotting hazards early so you can change before a crash. Remember: spot hazards, change early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Risk awareness is the ability to spot present and possible hazards, including other road users, weather and distractions, so you can change what you do before a crash.

question.text: How should you use your eyes while driving?

answer.text: Keep your eyes scanning all the time, using peripheral vision and mirrors to track what is ahead, beside and behind you.

teaching.text: Keep scanning ahead, beside and behind, using peripheral vision and mirrors. Remember: keep eyes moving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep your eyes scanning all the time, using peripheral vision and mirrors to track what is ahead, beside and behind you.

question.text: After spotting a hazard that needs a change, what do you check?

answer.text: After you spot a hazard that needs a change, check behind you, because traffic there affects what you can safely do.

teaching.text: After spotting a hazard that needs a change, check behind you first. Remember: check behind first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After you spot a hazard that needs a change, check behind you, because traffic there affects what you can safely do.

question.text: Can driving risk be removed completely?

answer.text: Risk can never be removed completely, but you can lower it by identifying hazards and adjusting how you drive.

teaching.text: Risk can never be removed, but you can lower it by spotting hazards and adjusting. Remember: lower risk, never zero.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Risk can never be removed completely, but you can lower it by identifying hazards and adjusting how you drive.

question.text: What is hazard perception?

answer.text: Hazard perception is scanning for risks and identifying them before they become problems, and it calls for attention, quick decisions and fitting reactions.

teaching.text: Hazard perception is scanning for risks and identifying them before they become problems. Remember: spot risks before problems.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hazard perception is scanning for risks and identifying them before they become problems, and it calls for attention, quick decisions and fitting reactions.

question.text: What counts as a hazard?

answer.text: A hazard is anything that makes you change speed or direction, from a child darting into the road to a trash can, a speed limit sign or your own driveway turn.

teaching.text: Anything that makes you change speed or direction is a hazard. Remember: anything forcing a change.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A hazard is anything that makes you change speed or direction, from a child darting into the road to a trash can, a speed limit sign or your own driveway turn.

question.text: Does a trash can count as a hazard?

answer.text: A hazard is defined by needing a change in your speed or direction, so a harmless trash can or an upcoming driveway counts just as a running child does.

teaching.text: A hazard is anything needing a change, even a trash can or your own driveway. Remember: change needed means hazard.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A hazard is defined by needing a change in your speed or direction, so a harmless trash can or an upcoming driveway counts just as a running child does.

question.text: What must a driver decide when several hazards appear at once?

answer.text: Hazards can be still or moving and can come several at once, and the driver must decide which one needs the most urgent response.

teaching.text: When several hazards appear, decide which needs the most urgent response. Remember: rank the hazards.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hazards can be still or moving and can come several at once, and the driver must decide which one needs the most urgent response.

question.text: How does spotting hazards differ from ranking them?

answer.text: Hazard perception is spotting risks before they become problems, while choosing which of several hazards needs the most urgent response is a separate driver duty.

teaching.text: Spotting hazards and ranking them are separate driver duties. Remember: spot, then rank.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hazard perception is spotting risks before they become problems, while choosing which of several hazards needs the most urgent response is a separate driver duty.

question.text: Why slow down as you approach hazards?

answer.text: Slow down as you approach hazards to gain space and time for safe decisions.

teaching.text: Slow down approaching hazards to gain space and time. Remember: slow down, gain time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down as you approach hazards to gain space and time for safe decisions.

question.text: What is situational awareness, and who may be most affected by your choices?

answer.text: Situational awareness is constantly watching everything around you and predicting what to prepare for, and the drivers behind you may be the ones most affected by your choices.

teaching.text: Situational awareness watches everything around you, including drivers behind. Remember: watch all around.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Situational awareness is constantly watching everything around you and predicting what to prepare for, and the drivers behind you may be the ones most affected by your choices.

question.text: What are the five steps of the hazard management routine?

answer.text: The hazard management routine has five steps in order: plan, communicate, check, execute and evaluate.

teaching.text: The routine is plan, communicate, check, execute and evaluate, in that order. Remember: plan, communicate, check, execute, evaluate.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The hazard management routine has five steps in order: plan, communicate, check, execute and evaluate.

question.text: What happens in the plan step?

answer.text: In the plan step you scan around you, including the rearview mirror, and decide whether the change you want is safe.

teaching.text: In the plan step, scan, including the rearview mirror, and decide whether the change is safe. Remember: plan: scan and decide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In the plan step you scan around you, including the rearview mirror, and decide whether the change you want is safe.

question.text: What happens in the check step?

answer.text: In the check step you set your position and speed so the change needs no more than medium braking, recheck mirrors, and look over your shoulder for walkers and cyclists.

teaching.text: In the check step, set position and speed for medium braking at most, then check mirrors and shoulder. Remember: check: position, mirrors, shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In the check step you set your position and speed so the change needs no more than medium braking, recheck mirrors, and look over your shoulder for walkers and cyclists.

question.text: Which step includes signaling, and which includes mirror and shoulder checks?

answer.text: Signaling belongs to the communicate step, while rechecking mirrors and looking over your shoulder belong to the check step that follows it.

teaching.text: Signaling is the communicate step; mirror and shoulder checks are the check step after it. Remember: signal, then check.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signaling belongs to the communicate step, while rechecking mirrors and looking over your shoulder belong to the check step that follows it.

question.text: What braking does the check step aim for?

answer.text: The check step aims for a change that needs at most medium braking, not hard braking, by setting your position and speed first.

teaching.text: The check step aims for medium braking at most, not hard braking. Remember: medium braking at most.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The check step aims for a change that needs at most medium braking, not hard braking, by setting your position and speed first.

question.text: What happens in the execute and evaluate steps?

answer.text: In the execute step you make the change smoothly without surprising anyone, and in the evaluate step you review how it went and adjust next time.

teaching.text: Execute the change smoothly, then evaluate how it went. Remember: smooth change, then review.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In the execute step you make the change smoothly without surprising anyone, and in the evaluate step you review how it went and adjust next time.

question.text: How does higher speed affect seat belts and scanning?

answer.text: Higher speeds make seat belts less effective and leave less time to scan for walkers, cyclists and other vehicles.

teaching.text: Higher speed makes belts less effective and leaves less time to scan. Remember: speed weakens belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Higher speeds make seat belts less effective and leave less time to scan for walkers, cyclists and other vehicles.

question.text: How does speeding affect control and stopping?

answer.text: Speeding cuts vehicle and traction control, especially in rain or snow, and lengthens the distance needed to stop.

teaching.text: Speeding cuts control, especially in rain or snow, and lengthens stopping distance. Remember: speed cuts control.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speeding cuts vehicle and traction control, especially in rain or snow, and lengthens the distance needed to stop.

question.text: How does speed affect crash impact?

answer.text: Crash impact force rises with speed, so injuries become more severe and deaths more likely.

teaching.text: Crash force rises with speed, making injuries worse and deaths more likely. Remember: more speed, more force.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Crash impact force rises with speed, so injuries become more severe and deaths more likely.

question.text: What is a speed limit, and what else does Washington law require?

answer.text: A speed limit is the highest legal speed under ideal conditions, and Washington law also requires a speed that is safe for current conditions.

teaching.text: The limit is for ideal conditions, and the law also requires a speed safe for conditions. Remember: limit is for ideal conditions.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A speed limit is the highest legal speed under ideal conditions, and Washington law also requires a speed that is safe for current conditions.

question.text: Is driving below the speed limit allowed?

answer.text: Driving below the speed limit is allowed, but going over it is illegal.

teaching.text: Driving below the limit is allowed; going over it is illegal. Remember: below allowed, above illegal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving below the speed limit is allowed, but going over it is illegal.

question.text: Is the posted speed limit a target?

answer.text: The posted limit is a ceiling for ideal conditions, not a target, so a slower speed can be legally required when the road, weather or traffic is poor.

teaching.text: The posted limit is a ceiling for ideal conditions, not a target. Remember: ceiling, not target.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The posted limit is a ceiling for ideal conditions, not a target, so a slower speed can be legally required when the road, weather or traffic is poor.

question.text: Where should you slow down?

answer.text: Slow down for sharp curves or hills with poor visibility, slippery roads, areas with pedestrians, children, cyclists or animals, parking lots, heavy traffic, narrow bridges and tunnels, and residential streets.

teaching.text: Slow for curves, slippery roads, people and animals, parking lots, bridges, tunnels and residential streets. Remember: slow for curves, crowds, lots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down for sharp curves or hills with poor visibility, slippery roads, areas with pedestrians, children, cyclists or animals, parking lots, heavy traffic, narrow bridges and tunnels, and residential streets.

question.text: Why do new drivers face higher risk in judging space?

answer.text: Judging space takes practice, which is why new drivers face higher risk, and space can be judged by either distance or time.

teaching.text: Judging space takes practice, and space can be judged by distance or time. Remember: space judging takes practice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Judging space takes practice, which is why new drivers face higher risk, and space can be judged by either distance or time.

question.text: How much gap should you keep behind the vehicle ahead?

answer.text: Near other vehicles, keep a gap to the vehicle ahead of at least twice the length of your own vehicle.

teaching.text: Keep at least two of your vehicle's lengths behind the vehicle ahead. Remember: two car lengths back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Near other vehicles, keep a gap to the vehicle ahead of at least twice the length of your own vehicle.

question.text: How is the following gap stated, and how may space be judged?

answer.text: The following gap in this guide is stated as at least two vehicle lengths behind the car ahead, and space may be judged by distance or by time.

teaching.text: The following gap is at least two vehicle lengths, judged by distance or time. Remember: two lengths; distance or time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The following gap in this guide is stated as at least two vehicle lengths behind the car ahead, and space may be judged by distance or by time.

question.text: How much room should you leave when merging?

answer.text: Merge with enough room that nobody around you must swerve, slow or stop, because squeezing into a small gap is dangerous if the car ahead brakes.

teaching.text: Merge with enough room that nobody has to swerve, slow or stop. Remember: merge without forcing anyone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Merge with enough room that nobody around you must swerve, slow or stop, because squeezing into a small gap is dangerous if the car ahead brakes.

question.text: Who has the right-of-way when you merge onto an interstate?

answer.text: Drivers already on the interstate have the right-of-way, so you adjust your speed up or down and use the whole on-ramp, your signal and mirrors to find a safe gap.

teaching.text: Traffic already on the interstate has the right-of-way, so use the ramp to find a gap. Remember: freeway traffic goes first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers already on the interstate have the right-of-way, so you adjust your speed up or down and use the whole on-ramp, your signal and mirrors to find a safe gap.

question.text: On an interstate on-ramp, who yields?

answer.text: On an interstate on-ramp the merging driver yields, because traffic already on the interstate holds the right-of-way.

teaching.text: On an interstate on-ramp, the merging driver yields. Remember: merging driver yields.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On an interstate on-ramp the merging driver yields, because traffic already on the interstate holds the right-of-way.

question.text: What does the guide say zipper merging does?

answer.text: The guide says zipper merging improves traffic flow by sixty percent and makes merging predictable, lowering the risk of crashes from sudden lane changes.

teaching.text: The guide says zipper merging improves flow by sixty percent and makes merging predictable. Remember: zipper keeps traffic moving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The guide says zipper merging improves traffic flow by sixty percent and makes merging predictable, lowering the risk of crashes from sudden lane changes.

question.text: In a zipper merge, when do you move over?

answer.text: In a zipper merge at a lane closure, keep using both lanes until you reach the marked merge area instead of moving over early.

teaching.text: In a zipper merge, use both lanes until the marked merge area. Remember: both lanes to the merge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a zipper merge at a lane closure, keep using both lanes until you reach the marked merge area instead of moving over early.

question.text: What do you do at the zipper merge point?

answer.text: At the merge point, take turns, let one car from the ending lane go in front of you, and keep a steady speed matching the open lane.

teaching.text: At the merge point, take turns and keep a steady speed matching the open lane. Remember: take turns, steady speed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At the merge point, take turns, let one car from the ending lane go in front of you, and keep a steady speed matching the open lane.

question.text: At a slow lane closure, should everyone move over early?

answer.text: At a slow lane closure the zipper method keeps both lanes in use up to the merge area, rather than everyone moving over early.

teaching.text: At a slow lane closure, the zipper method keeps both lanes in use to the merge area. Remember: zipper uses both lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a slow lane closure the zipper method keeps both lanes in use up to the merge area, rather than everyone moving over early.

question.text: What is eye-lead time?

answer.text: Eye-lead time is the defensive habit of scanning as far ahead and to the sides as you can, using mirrors for behind, so you see hazards early and act rather than react.

teaching.text: Eye-lead time means scanning far ahead and to the sides so you act rather than react. Remember: look far ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Eye-lead time is the defensive habit of scanning as far ahead and to the sides as you can, using mirrors for behind, so you see hazards early and act rather than react.

question.text: How can you practice judging time?

answer.text: To practice judging time, choose a marker you think is fifteen seconds ahead, then count until you reach it.

teaching.text: Practice judging time by counting to a marker you think is fifteen seconds ahead. Remember: pick a marker, count.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To practice judging time, choose a marker you think is fifteen seconds ahead, then count until you reach it.

question.text: How does the marker exercise differ from eye-lead time?

answer.text: The fifteen-second marker exercise trains you to estimate distance in seconds, while eye-lead time is the wider habit of scanning far ahead.

teaching.text: The marker exercise trains timing; eye-lead time is the wider scanning habit. Remember: drill versus habit.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The fifteen-second marker exercise trains you to estimate distance in seconds, while eye-lead time is the wider habit of scanning far ahead.

question.text: Why does having enough time matter in traffic?

answer.text: Having enough time lets you weigh and rank decisions in traffic, which reduces panic and impulsive moves.

teaching.text: Having enough time lets you rank decisions and reduces panic. Remember: time cuts panic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Having enough time lets you weigh and rank decisions in traffic, which reduces panic and impulsive moves.

question.text: Turning across oncoming traffic, who has the right-of-way?

answer.text: When turning across oncoming traffic, remember that approaching traffic has the right-of-way, and allowing too much time is better than too little.

teaching.text: Turning across traffic, oncoming traffic goes first, and too much time beats too little. Remember: oncoming first; extra time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When turning across oncoming traffic, remember that approaching traffic has the right-of-way, and allowing too much time is better than too little.

question.text: How do you judge a gap before turning?

answer.text: To judge a turn gap, count the seconds an oncoming car takes from a roadside marker to clear the road you want, then use that to estimate when the next car will arrive.

teaching.text: Judge a turn gap by counting seconds from a roadside marker. Remember: count from a marker.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To judge a turn gap, count the seconds an oncoming car takes from a roadside marker to clear the road you want, then use that to estimate when the next car will arrive.

question.text: Before a left turn across traffic, who yields, and what if the gap is uncertain?

answer.text: Before a left turn across traffic the turning driver yields, and when the gap is uncertain the guide favors waiting for extra time.

teaching.text: The turning driver yields and waits for extra time when the gap is uncertain. Remember: turner yields; wait if unsure.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before a left turn across traffic the turning driver yields, and when the gap is uncertain the guide favors waiting for extra time.
